name: AI phrase contamination in published papers (2023–2025)
dinh_nghia: AI phrase contamination refers to the presence of verbatim or near-verbatim LLM artifact phrases in published academic papers — phrases that betray the use of AI writing assistance without disclosure. Examples include 'As an AI language model, I...', 'As of my last knowledge update...', 'Certainly, here is a possible introduction for your topic', and 'Regenerate response'. These phrases indicate undisclosed AI use in manuscript preparation, violating disclosure norms and, in many cases, journal policies.
phan_loai: Undisclosed AI-assisted writing (academic dishonesty via omission of disclosure). Range from minor non-disclosure violations to research fraud when AI-generated content is factually incorrect or fabricated. Multiple subcategories: đạo văn (if AI text is used without attribution), gian lận AI (undisclosed AI use), and in severe cases bịa đặt (if AI-generated factual claims are false).
lich_su_khai_niem: AI phrase contamination emerged as a detectable phenomenon from November 2022 (ChatGPT public release). By early 2023, researchers and science journalists began compiling databases of papers containing telltale LLM phrases. Retraction Watch maintains a running list. The phenomenon peaked in 2024 as LLM use in academic writing became widespread and author disclosure practices remained inconsistent.
ten_truong_hop: Multiple incidents: (1) 115+ Google Scholar articles containing 'As an AI language model' or 'As of my last knowledge update' (2023-2024 database); (2) Springer 'Advanced Nanovaccines for Cancer Immunotherapy' book ($119, March 2025) — AI phrase on page 25; (3) Zhang et al. retraction, Surfaces and Interfaces (Elsevier, 2024) — AI artifact phrase in introduction; (4) Bader et al. retraction, Radiology Case Reports (2024) — AI phrase detected.
dien_bien: Beginning in 2023, researchers and science journalists began systematically searching Google Scholar and academic databases for papers containing characteristic LLM phrases. A database of 115+ papers containing phrases like 'As an AI language model, I can provide a general perspective' or 'As of my last knowledge update' was compiled. In one Elsevier journal (Surfaces and Interfaces), a paper titled 'The three-dimensional porous mesh structure of Cu-based metal-organic-framework — aramid cellulose separator enhances the electrochemical performance of lithium metal anode batteries' contained the phrase 'certainly, here is a possible introduction for your topic' in its introduction. The paper remained published for 38 days after discovery without correction. The Springer book 'Advanced Nanovaccines for Cancer Immunotherapy' by Nanasaheb Thorat (March 2025) was sold for $119-160 and contained on page 25: 'As an AI language model, I can provide a general perspective, but you should consult with medical professionals for personalized advice.' Springer withdrew the book and investigated. The author claimed to have received 'help' from colleagues and denied knowing how the AI phrase appeared. A broader study (Science/AAAS, 2024) of 1 million+ scientific papers found 22.5% of computer science abstracts showed evidence of LLM modification by September 2024.
ket_qua_xu_ly: Springer withdrew the cancer book and initiated investigation. Elsevier retracted the Surfaces and Interfaces paper. Multiple papers on the Retraction Watch 'ChatGPT writing evidence' list were retracted by their respective journals. No criminal prosecutions were reported. Individual journals issued retractions without consistent messaging about AI use policy. The Science/AAAS analysis noted that the frequency of AI-associated words like 'delve' subsequently declined — suggesting authors are now scrubbing detectable AI phrases, making detection harder.
con_so_thong_ke: 115+ Google Scholar papers identified containing verbatim LLM artifact phrases (2023-2024). 22.5% of CS paper abstracts showed LLM modification evidence by September 2024 (analysis of 1M+ papers). 1 book ($119 Springer title) withdrawn. Multiple individual journal retractions (exact count varies by database). The word 'delve' increased >3x in scientific abstracts post-ChatGPT launch before declining as it became recognized as an AI marker.
hai_cho_nguoi_hoc: Students and researchers reading contaminated papers receive information partly or wholly generated by AI without disclosure, making it impossible to assess the reliability of that information. AI-generated content may contain factual errors or hallucinations presented as expert knowledge. The Springer cancer book is particularly concerning given the medical advice context.
hai_cho_nghien_cuu: AI phrase contamination indicates systematic undisclosed AI use in manuscript preparation. Where AI content contains hallucinated facts or fabricated citations, the scientific record is corrupted. The scale — potentially 20%+ of CS papers by 2024 — represents a fundamental challenge to the integrity of the published record. Peer reviewers are not trained or incentivized to detect AI phrases, as demonstrated by publications that cleared review despite obvious artifacts.
hai_cho_xa_hoi: Medical information (cancer book), engineering research (materials science), and policy-relevant science contaminated with unverified AI content poses direct public safety risks. The Springer cancer book incident, had it not been flagged, could have provided harmful medical advice to patients who purchased it.
cong_cu_phat_hien: Primary detection method: keyword/phrase search in full-text databases for characteristic LLM artifact strings ('As an AI language model', 'Certainly here is', 'Regenerate response', 'As of my knowledge cutoff'). Retraction Watch maintains a curated list. Secondary: statistical analysis of word frequency shifts (Science/AAAS 2024 study). Tools like GPTZero can detect AI-generated text probabilistically but phrase searching is more reliable for obvious cases.
han_che_cong_cu: Phrase-based detection only catches unsophisticated cases where authors failed to remove LLM artifact text. Sophisticated AI-assisted writing that has been edited and cleaned is not detectable by phrase search. As noted by the Science/AAAS study, authors are already adapting — reducing 'delve' usage — suggesting an arms race between AI writing and detection. LLM watermarking would provide more reliable attribution.
watermarking: If LLMs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) implemented mandatory watermarking (Kirchenbauer/UMD scheme, Aaronson/OpenAI scheme), AI phrase contamination would be traceable to specific models and generation events. The Springer book incident demonstrates the value of such watermarking — provenance would be verifiable rather than inferred from artifact phrases.
thiet_ke_bai_tap: For academic assignments: requiring students to submit AI interaction logs/prompts alongside papers would make undisclosed AI use impossible. For journal submissions: mandatory AI-use declaration forms at submission, with penalties for false declarations. Automated phrase screening as part of submission processing.
chinh_sach_truong_hoc: Major journals updated AI disclosure policies after 2023: Nature Portfolio, Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley all now require authors to declare AI use in manuscript preparation. However, enforcement relies on author honesty — no automated verification is universal. Some journals (e.g., Science) prohibit AI-generated text in submissions entirely.
van_hoa_to_chuc: The scale of contamination (22.5% of CS papers by 2024) suggests the problem is systemic, not individual. A culture of disclosure must be built alongside detection. McCabe's honor code research: punitive-only approaches after the fact are insufficient when the behavior is this widespread — structural norms change is required.
ai_literacy: Authors who accidentally included AI artifact phrases in published papers demonstrate low AI literacy — specifically, not understanding that LLMs insert self-referential phrases or that these phrases are traceable. AI literacy in academic publishing must include: understanding LLM artifact patterns, disclosure obligations, and verification practices.
khung_quoc_te: EU AI Act (2024) Article 50 requires disclosure of AI-generated content. IEEE Code of Ethics and ACM Code of Ethics prohibit misrepresentation in scientific publications. ICMJE (International Committee of Medical Journal Editors) updated authorship guidelines to exclude AI as an author but require disclosure of AI use — directly relevant to medical publishing cases (cancer book, Radiology Case Reports).
phap_luat_viet_nam: Nghị định 109/2022/NĐ-CP Điều 20 requires integrity in scientific publication but does not specifically address AI disclosure. The absence of an explicit AI disclosure requirement in Vietnamese research law represents a regulatory gap. Luật KH&CN 2025 (if enacted) may address this.
chinh_sach_chau_a: CUHK (Hong Kong) and NUS (Singapore) have developed explicit AI disclosure frameworks. NTU imposed zero marks for work with AI-generated unreliable content. The Springer cancer book and Surfaces and Interfaces cases have been cited in Asian university policy updates.
ai_tutor_vs_ai_cheater: The spectrum of AI phrase contamination cases illustrates the AI-as-cheater risk: from careless non-disclosure to deliberate fraud. The distinction between AI as writing tool (legitimate) and AI as replacement for scientific thought (fraud) is central. Neil Selwyn's concern is validated — AI enables academic fraud at previously impossible scale.
edtech_company_policies: Elsevier (ScienceDirect), Springer Nature, and Wiley all added AI-content detection to their editorial systems post-2023. iThenticate/Turnitin updated to flag AI-characteristic phrases. Some EdTech platforms (Coursera, edX) require AI disclosure in submitted assignments.
de_xuat_nha_nghien_cuu: From an EdTech/research integrity perspective: (1) Automated AI phrase screening must be standard in all journal submission systems; (2) AI disclosure forms should be mandatory and signed (not just optional checkboxes); (3) LLM providers should implement output logging/watermarking to enable provenance verification; (4) The arms race dynamic (authors scrubbing AI phrases) requires systemic solutions — behavioral norms, not just detection; (5) Attribution standards must evolve: AI as a tool requires citation (e.g., 'Sections X-Y were drafted using [LLM], verified and revised by authors').
bai_bao_khoa_hoc: Science/AAAS (2024): 'One-fifth of computer science papers may include AI content' (science.org). Retraction Watch: 'Papers and peer reviews with evidence of ChatGPT writing' (running database). Pivot-to-AI (2025): '$119 Springer cancer treatments book: As an AI language model' (pivot-to-ai.com). Haider et al. (2024): GPT-fabricated papers HKS Misinformation Review. Scientific American: 'AI Chatbots Have Thoroughly Infiltrated Scientific Publishing.'

Vietnamese language papers on similar topics may exist in VNU Journal of Science, but none confirmed for this specific phenomenon.
